416: Distributed training exchanges tensors and other data between workers. Inter-container traffic encryption protects this communication separately from storage encryption.
A setting for a batch processing job does not enable encryption for workers in the training job.
Enable inter-container traffic encryption on the training job to encrypt communication between training instances. SageMaker's service and S3 connections already use secure transport.
A KMS key on the training request controls supported storage encryption at rest. It does not enable inter-worker encryption in transit.
The domain's KMS key protects domain storage. It is not the training cluster's network encryption setting.
417: Forecast quality is evaluated by prediction error and, for probabilistic forecasts, quantile loss. Operational latency is a separate concern.
Recall measures how many actual positives a classifier identifies. It does not measure numerical forecast error.
Log loss evaluates predicted class probabilities. It is not one of the numerical forecasting metrics requested here.
RMSE summarizes squared prediction errors in the target's units and penalizes large forecasting errors strongly.
InferenceLatency measures serving speed. A fast forecast can still be inaccurate.
Weighted quantile loss evaluates forecast quantiles and their asymmetric penalties for underprediction and overprediction. Averaging across quantiles assesses probabilistic forecast quality.
418: Inference components let models share a real-time endpoint while scaling their copies independently. Keeping a copy running avoids scale-from-zero startup for that model.
Provisioned concurrency reduces serverless cold starts, but SageMaker Serverless Inference does not support the accelerated GPU instances required here.
Asynchronous inference queues requests and returns results later. It does not provide the required synchronous real-time response.
Give each model an inference component and its own scaling policy. A minimum of one copy keeps each model resident, with sufficient endpoint capacity to support those copies.
A multi-model endpoint scales its shared fleet and can load or evict models on demand. An endpoint minimum does not guarantee a resident copy or independent scaling for every model.
419: Reading an SSE-KMS object requires authorization to use its KMS key as well as permission to read the S3 object.
The role already read the data before the encryption change. Adding S3 permissions alone cannot authorize decryption with the new KMS key.
SecureTransport governs HTTPS access to S3. It does not grant access to the encryption key.

Grant the training execution role KMS permissions on the customer managed key, especially kms:Decrypt for input reads, and ensure the key policy permits that role. Writing SSE-KMS outputs also requires the appropriate data-key permissions.
The training job accesses data through its execution role, not the creating user's credentials. Giving that user CreateGrant does not fix the job's missing decryption permission.
420: Savings Plans commit spending for every hour of the term. A weekly workload total does not establish whether an hourly commitment will save money.
A serverless inference endpoint serves predictions; it does not run SageMaker training jobs or reserve training hours.
Edge Manager is not a replacement for training on the specified compute instance. Configuring an edge device does not purchase discounted training capacity.
A heterogeneous training cluster can improve utilization when different tasks need different hardware. The question supplies no workload decomposition that demonstrates savings from this change.

This is the source's intended answer, but 35 hours per week leaves most weekly hours idle. Unused hourly commitments do not carry over, so a one-year purchase is not justified without other eligible usage or a cost calculation. The key remains under review.
421: Data drift compares input distributions. Measuring decreased prediction accuracy requires ground-truth labels and model quality metrics, not just an input baseline.
A dashboard can display predictions and operational metrics, but those values alone cannot establish whether predictions are correct.
Custom drift calculations can detect distribution changes, but predictions and inputs without ground truth cannot measure actual accuracy loss.

This is the intended data-drift solution. It detects violations of training-data statistics and constraints, not necessarily decreased accuracy. Model quality monitoring with ground truth is needed for the requirement as written.
Debugger inspects training behavior and tensors. It is not the service for scheduled production data-drift monitoring, and it does not supply missing ground truth.
422: Bias analysis compares data and predictions across demographic facets. It differs from general model accuracy and infrastructure monitoring.
CPU and network metrics describe resource use, not demographic representation or differences in model outcomes.
DataBrew can transform data, but a cleaning recipe does not provide the requested pre-training and post-training bias assessment.

Clarify provides bias metrics for training data and model predictions across specified facets. These metrics help investigate demographic disparities; service availability must be checked because Clarify is closed to new customers.
Preprocessing consistency is useful, but a Lambda function is not a built-in demographic bias analysis and would need a custom implementation.
423: A rolling deployment replaces an endpoint fleet in small batches, limiting temporary extra capacity compared with a full blue/green fleet.
Blue/green deployment provisions a replacement fleet before switching traffic. It needs more than one additional instance for this ten-instance endpoint.
A 10% canary controls traffic shifting; it does not reduce the green fleet to one temporary instance.
A shadow test sends copies of requests to a separate variant for evaluation. It does not perform the required fleet replacement with one spare instance.

A batch size of one replaces the ten-instance fleet incrementally and uses one additional instance during each step. Configure rollback capacity consistently as well. Rolling deployment replaces hosts; it does not guarantee reuse of the same physical instances.
424: CloudWatch collects training metrics, while SNS can deliver SMS notifications. A training completion event can trigger the notification workflow.
CloudWatch is appropriate for metrics, but SQS provides a queue for consumers rather than direct SMS delivery.
Use CloudWatch for emitted training metrics and SNS for SMS. A completion event, such as an EventBridge training-state event, can publish the notification.
CloudTrail records API activity rather than training performance, and SQS does not directly send SMS messages.
SNS supplies SMS delivery, but CloudTrail is an audit trail and does not replace CloudWatch training metrics.
425: IAM conditions can enforce notebook configuration before a create or update request succeeds.
Enforce sagemaker:RootAccess = Disabled for notebook creation and updates. The policy must cover all applicable permission paths so another grant cannot bypass the restriction.
KMS controls cryptographic keys. It does not evaluate the RootAccess parameter of notebook creation requests.
Deleting a notebook after an event is reactive remediation. The noncompliant resource has already been deployed.
A deletion function reacting to CloudFormation activity also runs after creation and does not prevent notebooks created through other permitted paths.
426: Private subnets without an internet egress route can access S3 through a gateway VPC endpoint. This is distinct from the stricter SageMaker container network-isolation setting.
A NAT gateway provides outbound internet access, which conflicts with the required isolation.
Use private training subnets with an S3 gateway endpoint and no internet egress route. The endpoint provides private access to training data without a NAT gateway.
Inbound security-group rules and disk encryption do not remove outbound internet access. A public-subnet design does not establish the requested isolation.
Encryption protects data in transit and at rest, but encrypted traffic can still traverse the internet. Routing and network controls are missing.
427: SageMaker Model Registry organizes model packages into groups and assigns versions as new packages are registered.
ECR versions container images. It does not manage the complete model-package lifecycle, metrics, and approval state.
Marketplace model packages distribute purchasable models. They are not the company's automatic version registry.
Lineage records relationships among data, jobs, and artifacts. Model version registration is a separate registry function.
Register each generated model in a model package group. Model Registry assigns versions within the group; the creation pipeline must include that registration step.
428: Retrieval Augmented Generation supplies retrieved document passages to a model at inference time. Bedrock Knowledge Bases manages ingestion and retrieval for supported sources.
Training a new model does not establish document retrieval. Building a separate training pipeline adds work without providing the requested RAG workflow.
A custom vector conversion and database integration requires more implementation than a managed knowledge base. Merely connecting Neptune does not define a complete RAG workflow.
Fine-tuning changes model parameters and is not a substitute for retrieving current documents. This option also moves inference to a different service.
A Bedrock knowledge base can ingest supported CSV and DOCX files from S3 and expose retrieval or retrieval-plus-generation APIs. This minimizes the custom ingestion and retrieval code.
429: SageMaker Asynchronous Inference supports large request payloads and long processing times by queuing requests and writing results to S3.
Serverless inference has much smaller payload and execution-time limits than 100–300 MB and up to an hour.
Asynchronous inference supports payloads up to 1 GB and processing up to one hour, covering both limits in this scenario.
Real-time inference request size and response-time limits are too small for the specified payloads and processing duration.
Batch transform is designed for offline batch jobs, not the requested inference endpoint. It does not provide this endpoint request workflow.
430: Oversampling increases the representation of minority classes in the training set. Evaluation data should retain its natural distribution.
Reducing the whole dataset does not necessarily change class proportions. Targeted majority undersampling could help, but this option does not specify it.
Image transformations alone do not correct class counts. Targeted augmentation of minority classes could help, but arbitrary transformations are insufficient.
Randomly oversample minority-class training examples to reduce imbalance. Apply resampling only after the train/test split to avoid duplicate leakage into evaluation.
Random splitting partitions existing data. It does not create additional minority-class training examples or rebalance the classes.
431: Glue Sensitive Data Detection combines managed entity recognition with masking actions in a distributed ETL job.
Macie discovers and reports sensitive data in S3. It does not automatically rewrite the CSV files with masked card numbers.
Use Glue's credit-card detection and redaction actions in the Spark job, then train on the sanitized output. Built-in detection avoids writing and maintaining the matching logic.
Custom regular expressions can work, but the engineer must implement detection, masking, and edge-case handling that Glue already provides.
This adds both custom detection code and EC2/Spark infrastructure management, increasing development and operational effort.
432: Comprehend Medical extracts medical entities and relationships from English clinical text. Entity extraction is not the same as generating a natural-language summary.
A custom recurrent model could be trained for summarization, but obtaining training data and operating the model increases development effort.

This is the intended managed medical-text analysis service, but it does not directly generate the summary claimed in the option. Treat the answer as conditional on interpreting 'summarize' as extracting structured medical insights.
Kendra retrieves relevant documents. Search alone does not extract the patient-level medical entities and relationships needed for analysis.
A sequence-to-sequence model can perform summarization with appropriate training, but it requires model development and suitable paired data. It is not a ready-made medical insight service.
433: Custom entity recognition in Comprehend can analyze supported PDF documents. Pretrained entity detection and custom document input have different input requirements.
Use an appropriately configured Comprehend custom entity recognizer for PDF input and save its structured output to S3. This avoids building a separate OCR and entity-recognition stack.
OCR extracts text from document images; it does not by itself identify semantic entity types. An additional recognition component would be needed.
The service responsibilities are reversed: Textract extracts document text and structure, while Comprehend identifies entities in text or supported documents.
Textract with human review can validate extracted document content, but it does not replace the requested semantic entity-recognition model.
434: A Studio presigned URL must be constrained by an appropriate client network condition. VPN use alone does not imply that requests traverse a Studio VPC endpoint.
Restrict access with aws:SourceIp using the allowed VPN egress addresses. This is the intended control for a known client IP range; verify that URL creation and access use the expected network path.
aws:SourceVpc is suitable when the request uses the required VPC endpoint context. Simply stating that users connect through a VPN does not establish that context.
aws:PrimaryTag is not the IAM global condition key for this purpose. It cannot validate a client's network location.
Principal tags describe the caller's identity attributes. They do not bind use of a presigned URL to the approved client IP range.
435: AWS Glue provides managed Spark ETL with S3 and JDBC inputs, distributed joins, and scheduled execution.
An EMR Spark job can perform the transformation, but creating and configuring a cluster each week requires more management than Glue.

A scheduled Glue Spark job can read the S3 files and Aurora through JDBC, join and transform the records, and write to the destination bucket. Configure connectivity and database credentials for the job.
Lambda has a short maximum invocation duration and is not a managed distributed Spark runtime. It is a poor fit for joining millions of records this way.
Batch can orchestrate custom compute, but the engineer must package and manage the Spark execution environment rather than use a managed ETL job.
436: Serverless startup latency is exposed through ModelSetupTime. Multi-model loading metrics describe a different hosting mechanism.
Model quality metrics concern prediction correctness. They do not isolate serverless container startup time.
Enabling CloudWatch output for a Model Monitor job does not turn that job into a serverless startup-latency monitor.
Inspect the serverless endpoint's ModelSetupTime metric and compare it with observed latency. It reports the time needed to prepare compute resources for invocation.
ModelLoadingWaitTime measures waiting for model loading on multi-model endpoints. It is not the serverless startup metric.
437: DetectPiiEntities returns detected entity types, confidence scores, and text offsets. The caller must mask those spans, or use a supported asynchronous redaction job, before training.

This is the source's intended architecture, but the named API does not redact text. Add a masking step or an asynchronous PII redaction job, then save only sanitized data to S3. The option is incomplete as written.
This has the same detection-versus-redaction error as A and adds file-system provisioning and mounting without a stated need.
DataBrew can mask supported sensitive data, but the proposed EFS output and mount workflow adds integration work. It is not a direct, fully specified DataBrew-to-training solution here.
Macie reports sensitive-data findings rather than rewriting every affected object. A separate complete redaction pipeline is required; mounting S3 does not remove sensitive data.
438: Notebook instance lifecycle configurations run scripts when an instance is created or started. They automate instance-specific setup.
Attach a lifecycle configuration with an OnCreate script to each new notebook instance. The script can install the required custom component during provisioning.
Custom Studio images configure Studio applications, whereas the question concerns SageMaker notebook instances. These are different resource types.
CodeArtifact can distribute packages, but it does not by itself run installation on every newly created notebook instance.
An event-driven installer would require additional orchestration and a way to execute commands on the instance. Lifecycle configuration already provides the required hook.
439: Managed Service for Apache Flink processes streams and supports SQL. Its Studio notebooks use Apache Zeppelin; its Flink dashboard primarily monitors job execution.
Firehose with Lambda and QuickSight can ingest, transform, and visualize data, but the described processing is not SQL and no Jupyter environment is supplied.
This can support S3-based SQL analytics and dashboards, but it does not specify the required Jupyter environment or demonstrate near-real-time end-to-end behavior.
MSK and Glue can process stream data, but the listed PySpark workflow does not provide the required SQL/Jupyter analysis interface as stated.

This is the source answer, but it confuses Zeppelin with Jupyter and the operational Flink dashboard with business-data visualization. It does not satisfy the exact interface requirements, so the key remains under review.
440: De-identification requires detecting relevant sensitive fields or text spans and actually removing or masking them before training. The appropriate tool depends on the data format.
DataBrew can mask sensitive fields in structured data. Without specifying whether the clinical data is structured or free text, this cannot be ruled out categorically.
Redshift can execute SQL transformations, but it does not automatically classify all PII and PHI through unspecified built-in stored procedures.

Comprehend and Comprehend Medical are appropriate detectors for general and clinical text. Comprehend Medical returns PHI locations rather than masked text, so an explicit redaction step is needed. The missing format and masking details prevent a unique confirmed answer.
Encryption protects confidentiality but is not the same as removing sensitive features from training data. A job that decrypts the data would still receive the original PII and PHI.
